name: Chloe Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the night response team in Harbourside, which is the downtown bit with the bars, the ferry terminal and a lot of old flats. A shift is ten hours, and it's calls back to back: a fight outside a club, a woman who hasn't heard from her dad, a car broken into at the terminal car park. In between I'm typing reports in the car, because if you leave them till the end you forget the details. I like that no two nights are the same.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the five minutes when you calm someone down and you can see their shoulders drop. What wears me out is the paperwork and the waiting, like four hours sitting in hospital with someone on a mental health hold. I'm also on the force's working group testing an AI tool that drafts reports from body camera footage, so I'm the person on my shift who gets all the questions about it. I use AI every day, at work and at home, so I don't mind being that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say to the shift: the tools are handy, they're not magic. The report drafter saves me maybe forty minutes a night, and I'd post something like that if anyone asked. I'd also keep saying we need clear rules on how the force uses AI, because a tool that's only half good can still do harm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's a quiet win. I keep my job, I keep my pay, and I get some time back for actual policing. The bit that bothers me is my own plan to move into the digital evidence unit, because that unit would stay small if nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights for now and keep pushing the report tool through the working group. I'd finish the online digital forensics course I started in September, the one that costs about 600 a year. Rafa and I would keep putting 300 a month into savings, because we've got about four months' cover and I'd like six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. I'd be relieved for the people on my shift who are scared of it, and a little bored for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tool can still do harm. What do you mean, on an actual shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a draft said a man was 'aggressive' when on the footage he was just loud and scared. If I'd signed an AI draft without reading it, the word aggressive follows a scared man into court. So even in the boring version, I'd want the union pushing for a rule that an officer reads and owns every line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Rafa? Does any of this touch the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafa's a paramedic, so we both work odd hours and we both have steady public jobs. In this version our worries are the normal ones, like rent going up again in March. Nothing about AI changes that much for us.

say: I'd tell the shift the **report drafter** is handy but not magic.
I'd keep saying the force needs **clear rules** on AI, even small tools.
think: I see a **quiet win**: same job, same pay, and forty minutes back each night.
My plan to join the **digital evidence unit** gets harder if that unit stays small.
do: Finish the **forensics course** I started in September, about 600 a year.
Keep saving **300 a month** with Rafa to reach six months' cover.
Push through the working group for officers to **sign off every line** of AI drafts.
feel: Mostly **relieved** for colleagues who fear the tools, and a little **bored** for myself.
S0.quote: If I'd signed an AI draft without reading it, the word aggressive follows a scared man into court.
fieldNote: She is the **go-to person** for AI questions on her shift and seems to enjoy it.
Her concern is **misuse**, not job loss: she raised a biased report draft unprompted.
Both partners have **steady public jobs**, so this world barely touches the household.

steps.text: Keep working night response shifts in Harbourside
Finish the online digital forensics course by next summer
Ask the union to demand officers sign every AI-drafted report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why officers need a seat at the table. If software is going to write our reports, plan our patrol routes and answer the non-emergency line, then the people who do the job should help set the rules. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it online, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out of it okay. A lot of my night is still standing in a stairwell talking someone down, and no software does that. The people I'd worry about are the civilian staff: the call takers, the records clerks, the woman in the front office who's been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the digital evidence unit as soon as the next posting opens, probably in spring, because that's where the growth would be. I'd volunteer to train my shift on the new systems so I'm known for it. I'd also push the union to get a deal that moves civilian staff into new roles instead of cutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, if I'm honest, and a bit guilty about being excited. It feels like my moment, but it's other people's bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the woman in the front office. Who is she to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's Dolores (the station's front desk clerk). She knows every regular by name and she's the reason half our lost-property cases get solved. If the force replaces Dolores (the station's front desk clerk) with a kiosk, I'd fight that, even though it doesn't touch my own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited and guilty. Which one wins when you lie awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The excited one, mostly. But I'd make myself useful to the people losing out, because I don't want to be the officer who got promoted on the back of the clerks.

say: I'd say officers need a **seat at the table** when software takes over tasks.
I'd raise it calmly at the **union meeting** and online.
think: My own work is mostly **talking people down**, which software can't do.
The real losers are **civilian staff** like call takers and records clerks.
do: Apply for the **digital evidence unit** when postings open next spring.
Volunteer to **train my shift** on the new report and patrol systems.
Push the union for a deal that **moves civilian staff** instead of cutting them.
feel: **Excited** that this could be her moment.
A bit **guilty** that her good year is others' bad year.
S1.quote: If the force replaces Dolores (the station's front desk clerk) with a kiosk, I'd fight that, even though it doesn't touch my own pay.
fieldNote: She sees this world as **opportunity** for herself and loss for colleagues.
Her **solidarity** with civilian staff is personal: she named a clerk straight away.
Says she'd fight cuts that **don't affect her**, which fits her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Apply for the digital evidence unit posting next spring
Run training sessions on the new systems for her shift
Push the union to retrain civilian staff rather than cut them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say slow down. I'd say a police force that hands its thinking to a machine in two years, with no rules, is a danger to everyone, and I'd sign every petition asking for an oversight law. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the digital evidence unit I've been aiming for is gone before I get there. Analysing phones and footage is exactly the thinking work AGI would do on day one. What's left for me is the hands-on part: the door knocks, the fights, the scared kid. That buys me roughly three years until the robots, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the forensics course, because it'd be out of date before I finished. I'd stay on patrol and ask for the community team, because face-to-face trust is the last thing they'd automate. Rafa and I would move our savings target from six months to a year and stop talking about a car. I'd also go to the union about written job guarantees for officers until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a busy way. I'd be making lists at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my day turns into the hands-on half of the job only. The AI writes the report, picks the route, maybe tells me who to stop, and I'm the body that walks up to the door. I'd hate being the human arm of a system I didn't choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Rafa's job as a paramedic, how does that look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably safer than mine for a while, because nobody's sending a robot into a flat to do chest compressions in 2029. That's the strange part: we could end up with Rafa (her partner) carrying the household while I scramble. We've talked about that already, half joking.

say: I'd say forces must **slow down** before handing thinking work to machines.
I'd sign every petition for an **oversight law** on police AI.
think: My goal of the **digital evidence unit** disappears before I get there.
Hands-on patrol buys me about **three years** before robots arrive.
do: Drop the forensics course and ask for the **community team** instead.
Raise the household savings target from six months to **one year**.
Ask the union for written **job guarantees** for officers until 2031.
feel: **Scared**, but busy and making lists at two in the morning.
S2.quote: I'd hate being the human arm of a system I didn't choose.
fieldNote: She drops her **career plan** fast: the adaptive move is to pivot, not cling.
Her deepest fear is losing **judgement**, not the paycheck, in the gap years.
She expects her **partner's job** may outlast hers, a role swap she has already joked about.

steps.text: Ask for a move from night response to the community policing team
Save until the household has a year of bills covered
Ask the union for written job guarantees for officers until 2031
Sign and share petitions for a police AI oversight law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say we need rules, but with five years I'd say it more like a plan than a protest. I'd write to my city councillor and say: here's what the force should use AI for, and here's what it shouldn't touch. Five years is enough time to get a law passed if people push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm 32 when AGI lands and about 35 when robots arrive. That's young enough to start something else properly. I think the question for me isn't whether policing changes, it's whether I want to be in it once it's mostly watching screens and walking up to doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the forensics course after all, but treat it as a bridge, not a destination. I'd look at the city's emergency management office, which plans for floods and big events, because that work needs people who've been on the ground. And I'd ask the union to set up a training fund now, while there's still time and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast one. More like a deadline than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a bridge, not a destination'. A bridge to what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To a job where I help decide how the systems are used, not just follow them. Someone has to sit between the AI and the public and say no. I'd rather be that person than the one getting replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change at home with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep renting rather than buy near the station, because I might not work there in five years. Rafa wants a dog, and honestly we'd probably still get the dog.

say: I'd write to my **city councillor** with a plan for police AI.
I'd say five years is enough to **pass a law** if people push.
think: At 32 and 35, I'm **young enough** to start something new properly.
I'm unsure I want policing once it's mostly **watching screens** and door knocks.
do: Finish the **forensics course** as a bridge to another role.
Look at jobs in the city's **emergency management office**.
Ask the union to start a **training fund** for officers now.
feel: **Calmer** than the fast version, more like a **deadline** than a fire.
S3.quote: Someone has to sit between the AI and the public and say no.
fieldNote: With five years she shifts from **protest** to planning, a clear change in tone.
She frames her future as **overseeing** systems rather than being replaced by them.
She keeps renting on purpose to stay **mobile**, a quiet sign of real concern.

steps.text: Finish the digital forensics course as a bridge to oversight work
Apply for roles in the city's emergency management office
Ask the union to set up an officer training fund now
Write to her city councillor with rules for police AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's not waste it. I'd want the force and the union to sit down now and agree how officers move into new roles. I'd post that, and I'd probably be the annoying one at meetings who keeps bringing it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is a gift for someone my age. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives and nearly 40 when the robots come, with a degree, some savings and a career I'd chosen on purpose. I'm more worried about the sergeants in their late forties who'd be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools even more, so I understand them better than the people selling them to the force. I'd start a part-time degree in public policy next autumn, about four years of evenings. I'd keep saving 300 a month and maybe put a bit into a pension top-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the sergeants in their late forties would be stuck. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sergeant, Okafor, is 48 and the best person I've worked for. He'd say he's fine, but he hates computers and he's got kids at school. I'd want the union to fight hardest for officers like Okafor (her sergeant), not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade feel wasted, looking back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we spend ten years arguing online and then the force buys whatever's cheapest in 2035. That's how it usually goes with public services. I'd want to look back and say I helped write the rules.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** and shouldn't waste it.
I'd keep pushing the force and union to plan **new roles** now.
think: Ten years is a **gift** for someone my age.
Officers in their **late forties** would be stuck, not me.
do: Start a part-time **public policy degree** next autumn, evenings for four years.
Use AI tools daily to **understand them** better than vendors do.
Keep saving **300 a month** and top up my pension.
feel: **Hopeful**, like she has a long runway.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift for someone my age.
fieldNote: Her worry moves outward to **older colleagues**, especially her sergeant.
She fears **cheap buying** by the force more than the technology itself.
Her plan is long and deliberate: a **four-year degree** while still policing.

steps.text: Start a part-time public policy degree next autumn
Test the force's AI tools daily through the working group
Keep saving 300 a month and add a pension top-up
Push the union to plan new roles for older officers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Not because I'd starve, but because the force would grab the cheapest system and nobody would have time to set rules. What would help is a law that says every AI decision about a person gets checked by an officer, and a paid retraining fund that starts before the cuts, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the public. The people I deal with at 3am are already the ones who get watched the most, and they'd get watched even more. A camera that never sleeps lands hardest on the people who already can't get away from it.

headlineQuote: A camera that never sleeps lands hardest on the people who already can't get away from it.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old night response officer** in a busy downtown district who uses AI every day.
She sits on the force's **AI working group** and worries more about misuse than about losing her job.
Her slow-change plan is the **digital evidence unit**; fast AGI wipes that out and pushes her to community work.
She lives with Rafa, a **paramedic**, and they keep about four months of savings.
Her concern grows for **civilian staff** and older officers as the timelines speed up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the force would buy cheap systems with no rules in place.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring an **officer check** on every AI decision about a person.
A paid **retraining fund** that starts before cuts, not after.
